name: github-stars-organizer
description: Search your GitHub stars before suggesting a library; sort and prune stars
readme:
Stard

A card battle built from your GitHub stars

Every repo you've starred is a card. Build a team and beat other developers. No signup, free and open source.

Make your profile · npm · Agent API · Self-host

Here to organize your stars? Stard also sorts them into GitHub Lists and flags the dead ones. See the organizer

- Type a GitHub username, no sign-in. The shop deals cards from that account's stars, shuffled afresh for every run. - Buy cards onto your Drafts shelf, drag them onto your half of the board, then press **Fight**. Every card acts at once. - Cards that share a language or topic make a set, ticked off like a pull request's checks. After rounds 2 and 4 you pick one of three boosts. - 5 wins finishes a run, 3 losses ends one. ## Profile cards

Put in any GitHub username, no sign-in. If you like Stard, a star helps others find the project.

Your stars say what you actually use, and nobody can see them. Stard turns them into something for your GitHub profile: your top four repos, short reviews in your own words, and your Lists, each drawn as a card. **1. Pick your top four.** The four repos you would put on a poster. Every repo gets a poster in the colour of its language, filled up to a line that tracks how busy the repo was over the past year: a repo winding down drains to grey. **2. Review what you use.** A rating out of five and a sentence or two. The card links to the repo.

**3. Show your Lists.** Each GitHub List becomes a card, with the repos folded underneath. Archived and quiet repos are left out, so the list doesn't send people to dead projects.

**4. Copy the Markdown into your README.** The cards are plain images served from a link, so there is nothing to install or keep running. Paste them into the README of the repo named after your username and they show on your GitHub profile. Three ways to make one: - **In the browser.** Open the [demo](https://stard.armanckeser.com/compose), type your username and press **Load**, arrange the sections, copy. - **With your agent.** `npx skills add armanckeser/stard`, then ask Claude Code or Codex to "make my Stard profile". The agent asks which repos are your favorites and why, and writes the README with you. The **Profile** screen has a copy-paste prompt for agents without skills. - **On your own machine.** `npx github-stars-organizer` runs the full app on localhost with your [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com/) login (`gh auth login`). Ratings and notes you already keep there become your reviews. ## Your 2026 in stars

Every year-in-review sums up commits. This one sums up what you starred. Open `https://stard.armanckeser.com/wrapped/`: no sign-in, public stars only. - How many repos you starred this year, and the month you starred most. - Your top three languages. - Your earliest find: the most-starred repo you starred within 30 days of its creation. - How many of the year's stars are still alive: pushed to in the last 90 days and not archived. The page has a card for your README, buttons to post it on X or Bluesky, and a link to sort those stars into Lists. Stars are read once a day and counted by UTC month; a year past 1,000 stars shows as "1,000+". ### Option A: npx (recommended) Needs Node.js 20+ and the [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com/) logged in. Nothing to host: ```bash npx github-stars-organizer ``` ### Option B: self-host with Docker Needs Docker and a [classic token](https://github.com/settings/tokens/new?scopes=repo&description=Stars%20Organizer) with the `repo` scope, which is what lets Stard edit your Lists and unstar repos. Stard never reads or changes code; the key icon beside **Import Stars** shows which account and scopes the app is using. No clone: ```bash GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_... docker compose -f oci://ghcr.io/armanckeser/github-stars-organizer-stack:latest up -d ``` Open http://localhost:8080 and press **Import Stars**. That runs three containers (the app, Postgres and Electric); `ghcr.io/armanckeser/github-stars-organizer:aio` is all three in one, with its data under `/data`: ```bash docker run -d -p 8080:8080 -v stars-data:/data -e GITHUB_TOKEN=ghp_... ghcr.io/armanckeser/github-stars-organizer:aio ``` The token can unstar repos and edit your Lists, so anyone who can reach the port can too. Set `AUTH_PASSWORD` to require a password, or sign in through your OIDC provider (Authentik, Authelia, Pocket ID...) with `AUTH_ENABLED=1` and the `OIDC_*` settings in [docker-compose.selfhost.yml](docker-compose.selfhost.yml). Or leave both unset behind a proxy that already checks who gets in. **From your server's app store:** add the catalog once, then install Stard like any other app. | Server | Where | Paste | | --- | --- | --- | | Cosmos | Market → Sources → Add Source | `https://armanckeser.github.io/selfhost-apps/servapps.json` | | CasaOS / ZimaOS | App Store → Add Source | `https://github.com/armanckeser/selfhost-apps/archive/refs/heads/casaos.zip` | | Runtipi | Settings → App Stores → Add App Store | `https://github.com/armanckeser/selfhost-apps` | | Portainer | Settings → App Templates → URL | `https://armanckeser.github.io/selfhost-apps/portainer/templates.json` | Unraid's Community Apps doesn't list it yet; [selfhost-apps](https://github.com/armanckeser/selfhost-apps#add-the-catalog-to-your-server) has the template to add by hand. Umbrel isn't listed: Umbrel installs take no settings, and Stard needs the token. An AI agent can act through the same API as the UI (`/api/*`). With sign-in on, it sends `Authorization: Bearer `; set that yourself, or read the one generated on first start from the `instance_secret` table. [AGENT-API.md](AGENT-API.md#self-hosted) lists the routes. ## It also organizes the stars Stard started as Stars Organizer, and everything from it is still here. I starred hundreds of repos over the years and could never find anything again. GitHub has Lists now, but sorting 500 stars into them one dropdown at a time is pretty much nobody's idea of a weekend, and a good chunk of what I had starred was dead anyway. Stard lets Claude Code or Codex do the sorting, writes the Lists back to GitHub, and gives every repo a health score so the abandoned ones stand out.

## Compared with the alternatives | | GitHub's stars page | [Astral](https://astralapp.com) | [GithubStarsManager](https://github.com/AmintaCCCP/GithubStarsManager) | Stard | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Organizes with** | Lists, by hand | Tags, by hand | Its own categories, sorted by an AI with your API key | GitHub Lists, sorted by the Claude Code or Codex you already use | | **Shows up on GitHub** | Yes | No, tags live in Astral | Yes, Lists sync both ways | Yes, Lists sync both ways | | **Flags dead repos** | No | No | No | Health score per repo, plus active alternatives for dead ones | | **Tags, notes, ratings** | No | Tags and notes | Tags | Tags, notes and 1–5 ratings | | **Extras** | | Rule-based filters | Semantic search, release tracking, repo Q&A | Explore charts of what you starred over time, backups before every launch | | **How you run it** | Built in | Hosted, or self-host (PHP) | Desktop app or Docker | `npx`, or Docker | Based on each project's README and website as of November 2026. Coming from Astral? Stard imports Astral's export: tags become Lists and notes carry over. ## What's inside | | | |---|---| | **Lists** | Your GitHub Lists, plus a "Not in any list" pile to sort. Every change syncs back to GitHub. | | **Health score** | 0 to 10 from last commit, closed vs open issues, contributors, star growth and last release. Archived repos score 0. | | **Similar repos** | For any star, and active alternatives for the ones nobody maintains anymore. | | **Tags, ratings, notes** | On top of your stars, searchable and filterable. | | **Explore** | Charts of your stars by language, health and last commit, and what kinds of repos you starred over time. | | **Profile** | Your top four, your reviews and your Lists as cards for a GitHub README, with archived and quiet repos left out. Copy or download the Markdown. | | **Play** | A run in the browser: buy cards drawn from your stars, place them on a board, build sets and pick boosts, and fight other teams, until 5 wins or 3 losses. [Play one](https://stard.armanckeser.com/run). | | **Battle** | Two GitHub usernames, and each one's team of four (an ace they pick and three drawn from their stars each day) fights as trading cards in an arena: level from stars, HP from contributors, attack from commits, type from the language. A repo you own is shiny. Build a character on the Profile screen (a figure, a class with a perk, a motto), paste its card into your README, and the game reads your character from there. From your own copy you can challenge someone to a real match: turn by turn, over hours or days, with a GitHub Discussion on your profile repo as the whole record. Every move is a comment, the dice are public, and nothing is stored anywhere else. [Try one](https://stard.armanckeser.com/battle). The plan for the full game, played in GitHub Discussions, is in [#45](https://github.com/armanckeser/stard/issues/45). | | **AI sorting** | Claude Code, Codex or any agent that can run `curl` reads your stars, suggests Lists and sorts repos into them once you agree. The robot icon beside **Import Stars** gives you the prompt, or install the skill with `npx skills add armanckeser/stard`. [AGENT-API.md](AGENT-API.md) has the API. | | **Search for your agent** | `npx github-stars-organizer search pdf parser` lists the stars that match, with their Lists and whether each is still alive. To have Claude Code or Codex check your stars before suggesting a library or tool, add this line to your `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`: "Before you suggest a library, tool or GitHub repo, run `npx github-stars-organizer search ` to check what I already starred. If my pick is quiet or hasn't released in a year, say so and name the current alternative." | | **Backups** | A backup before every launch, and a restore that only adds back what's missing. | | **Private** | Your token never leaves your machine. No telemetry. Matches, team links and README cards use stard.armanckeser.com. |


Lists. The same table inside a List, with a health score on every repo.

## Is this for you? **Yes, if** you have a few hundred stars you never look at, you already use (or want to use) GitHub Lists, or you want to know which of your stars quietly died. **Not yet, if** you want semantic search over READMEs or release notifications (GithubStarsManager does both), or a hosted site you sign into (Astral has one). ## Contributing [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) has the dev setup. skillMd:
---
name: github-stars-organizer
description: Search the user's GitHub stars before suggesting a library, tool or repo, sort the stars into GitHub Lists, and find and unstar abandoned or archived ones, through Stard. Use whenever you are about to recommend or pick a library, framework, CLI tool or GitHub repo for the user, when the user wants to organize, categorize, clean up or search their GitHub stars or Lists, and when the user wants a Stard profile: their top four repos, reviews and Lists as cards for their GitHub profile README.
---

# Organize GitHub stars

## Check the user's stars before suggesting a tool

Before you recommend or pick a library, framework, CLI tool or repo, look in the
user's stars first. They starred these to use them later:

```bash
npx github-stars-organizer search <a few words>
```

Use two to four plain words for the job, like `pdf parser` or `self hosted photo`. Each
result shows the repo's Lists and whether it is active, `QUIET` (no push in 6 months)
or `ARCHIVED`. Start from an active star that fits, and say it's one they starred. If
the best match is quiet or archived, or its last release is over a year old, say so
and check whether a current alternative has overtaken it before you recommend it. The
user wants their own picks first, but not stale ones. If nothing fits, suggest
something else as usual. The search reads a copy on disk and needs no running server; the first
search of the day reads from GitHub and takes about 30 seconds for 500 stars. Add
`--json` for machine-readable output.

If the user wants this every time, offer to add this line to their `CLAUDE.md` or
`AGENTS.md`, since a skill isn't always loaded at the moment a tool is picked:
Before you suggest a library, tool or GitHub repo, run `npx github-stars-organizer search <a few words>` to check what I already starred. If my pick is quiet or hasn't released in a year, say so and name the current alternative.

Stard runs on the user's machine and serves an HTTP API at
`http://127.0.0.1:5185/api/local`. Changes go straight to the user's GitHub account, so
show a plan and wait for the user's OK before any write.

## Make the user's Stard profile

A Stard profile is a block for the user's GitHub profile README: their top four repos, a few short reviews, and their Lists, drawn as cards. The cards are images whose address holds what they show, so nothing has to be running. Read the "Profile cards" section of AGENT-API.md (https://github.com/armanckeser/stard/blob/main/AGENT-API.md#profile-cards) for the addresses and the Markdown.

The profile is the user's taste, so get the content by asking, one question at a time:

1. Their GitHub username, unless `gh api user --jq .login` already gives the name.
2. "Which four repos would you put on a poster?" If they want help remembering, run `npx github-stars-organizer search <words>` or show their most recent stars, but never choose for them.
3. For each of the four, a rating out of 5 if they want ratings shown.
4. "Which repos would you rave about, or warn people off?" For each: a rating and a sentence or two in their own words. Keep their wording. Do not write or pad a review; offer to tidy a review only when asked. Three reviews is plenty.
5. Whether they want a character for the battle game. If yes: a name, a motto, and a class (maintainer, scout, collector, specialist, veteran or archivist; say what each perk is). The look is easiest to build on the Profile screen at https://stard.armanckeser.com/compose; offer that, or pick the six numbers with them.
6. Which of their GitHub Lists to show, and in what order. Leave private Lists out unless they name one. Leave archived repos out of every List.

Then build the Markdown, show the whole block, and wait for a yes. Offer two ways to place the block: they paste the Markdown themselves, or you put the block in the `README.md` of the repo named after their username (create that repo, public, only with their OK; keep everything the README already holds, and replace an earlier Stard block rather than adding a second one). Tell them a card that changed can take a few hours to refresh on GitHub.

## Start it

1. Check whether it is already running: `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:5185/`.
2. If not, start it in the background with `npx github-stars-organizer --no-open`. It needs
   Node 20+ and a GitHub CLI login (`gh auth login`) or `GITHUB_TOKEN`. Each launch backs
   up the user's stars and Lists first.

The full API is in
[AGENT-API.md](https://github.com/armanckeser/stard/blob/main/AGENT-API.md).
Every request except `GET` needs `Content-Type: application/json`, including `DELETE`.

## Sort stars into Lists

1. `POST /import` with `{}` returns `{repos, lists}`, read live from GitHub.
2. Find the repos that are in no List. Suggest a List for each, reusing the user's Lists
   and proposing new ones only where several repos share a theme.
3. Show the plan as a table (repo, List, new or existing List) and wait for the user's OK.
4. Create new Lists with `POST /lists` `{name, description}`, then add repos with
   `POST /membership` `{repoNodeId, repoGithubId, githubListId, change: "add"}`.

## Clean up abandoned stars

1. `POST /health` with `{repos: [{node_id, stars, health_refreshed_at: null}]}` scores
   repos 0 to 10. It takes about a second per 20 repos.
2. List archived repos and low scores with their last push date, and let the user pick.
3. Unstar only the repos the user named: `POST /unstar` `{owner, name}`.

Tags, ratings and notes live in the browser, so the API can't read or change them.

## Self-hosted installs

A self-hosted Stard serves a different API under `/api` on its own address,
with `Authorization: Bearer <AGENT_API_TOKEN>` when sign-in is on. Ask the user for the
address and follow the "Self-hosted" section of AGENT-API.md.
